A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same subject-driven video generation framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark comparisons, component ablations, FVD motion evaluations, qualitative generations, and a 30-participant human study.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds gradient measurements, PCGrad comparisons, image-data ablations, and OpenS2V evaluation.

M1.justification: The default method retains CogVideoX-5B with LoRA, identity injection from image pairs, I2V motion preservation, stochastic task switching, random reference-frame selection, image-token dropping, and the reference token. Dual-task/replay terminology and expanded implementation details do not establish a changed default algorithm; PCGrad is evaluated as an alternative.

E1.justification: v2 adds the OpenS2V single-domain evaluation, including facial-identity assessment, and dedicated human-face success/failure cases in Figure 8. This broadens evaluation beyond v1's reference-image customization and Pexels motion tests. Subject200K and Pexels remain the training sources; their smaller subsets are setting changes.

E2.justification: Phantom and VACE using Wan-2.1-1.3B join the retained VBench comparators in v2 Table 2. CustomCrafter gains actual qualitative comparisons, PCGrad variants are evaluated in Table 5, and Table 12 adds comparisons with systems including Pika, Kling, SkyReels, HunyuanCustom, and larger model variants.

E3.justification: The stated learning-rate schedule changes from cosine annealing to cosine-with-restarts. v2 introduces a further-trained 16-FPS variant, 2K/4K image-subset experiments, and specifies the 4K-image model for Appendix D ablations. New protocols include held-out gradient measurements, PCGrad buffer sizes, and OpenS2V metrics such as FaceSim and NexusScore. These reported changes do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds gradient-direction and norm analyses comparing dual-task and image-only training, buffered-PCGrad comparisons, image-dataset-size sensitivity experiments, and human-face failure cases. The reference-token, video-count, switching-probability, and frame-selection/drop studies already existed in v1 and should not be counted as wholly new analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix B.1 newly specifies a fixed evaluation seed and reuse of validation batches for gradient measurements. Neither version reports independent repeated-run counts or confidence intervals. v2's statement that PCGrad differences fall within experimental variance is not accompanied by variance estimates.

E6.justification: The default row changes from v1 Table 1 to v2 Table 2: dynamic degree 60.19 to 69.64, DINO-I 59.29 to 62.88, and motion smoothness 98.72 to 98.45. Changed settings prevent treating these as isolated same-setting gains. v2 adds extensive baseline, PCGrad, subset, gradient, and OpenS2V results, including Total Score 50.05%. The human-study and FVD values remain unchanged in Tables 10 and 11.

T1.justification: v2 introduces Proposition 4.1 and Appendix C's formal assumptions, local quadratic analysis, dual-task and image-only convergence propositions, and PCGrad perturbation lemma with proofs. v1 contains method equations and motion definitions but no corresponding theoretical results.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes zero-shot generation without paired subject-video data and superiority over its baselines. v2 makes gradient independence a central contribution and adds explicit claims of 35–730-fold lower training cost and effectiveness with 50-fold fewer image pairs. Its abstract emphasizes competitive quality against substantially more resourced methods.

C2.justification: v2 interprets near-zero gradient cosine as independent identity/motion parameter directions and argues that explicit gradient surgery offers limited benefit. It adds explanations of small-subject failures in image-to-video pipelines and limitations involving human faces, centered training objects, and theoretical assumptions. OpenS2V discussion additionally addresses weak motion and facial-identity scores.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B substantially expand reproducibility information: LoRA target layers and scaling, token/view-drop probabilities, 720×480 preprocessing, 49-frame sequences, optimizer betas, warmup, gradient clipping, checkpointing, and distributed gradient logging. Appendix F documents assumptions and calculations behind baseline compute estimates. These disclosures exceed v1's comparatively brief implementation description without necessarily indicating changed underlying procedures.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against newer video systems, including Phantom, VACE, and HunyuanCustom, and introduces OpenS2V and Phantom-Data references. A new multi-task optimization subsection connects the framework to PCGrad, continual learning, and replay, changing the research context beyond v1's image/video customization discussion.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method exposition are substantially rewritten around dual-task learning and efficiency. S2V/S2I terminology becomes SDV-Gen/SDI-Gen. The appendix is reorganized into sections A–G, and retained human-study and temporal-evaluation material moves out of the main text.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the overview into separate dual-task and training/inference diagrams, redesigns the teaser and comparison montages, and restructures the main benchmark table into method groups. It adds compute and OpenS2V tables, gradient plots, and failure-case displays. Existing ablation figures and human/FVD tables are also relocated.

improvement.justification: Broader comparisons, OpenS2V testing, data-efficiency experiments, and implementation and limitation details strengthen the empirical paper. However, v2 makes gradient independence central while Appendix C incorrectly infers cosine convergence from inner-product decay. New interpretation errors also matter: Appendix E.3 calls FaceSim 18.05 similar to Phantom-1.3B's 44.03 in Table 12. These substantial benefits and new justification problems prevent a confident judgment of net overall improvement.
